#OTD in 1899, a man named S. R. Wharton wrote to the governor of New York proposing to launch him at the presidency. The governor forwarded the letter to a friend with one sentence of verdict.

"I send you the enclosed from S. R. Wharton. It seems to me that such a movement as he suggests would be altogether premature and ill-advised."

Premature is the word to notice. Wharton's letter does not survive, but Elting Morison, who edited Roosevelt's correspondence, judged he was proposing a campaign for 1904 — five years out. Roosevelt had been governor for nine months; eighteen months before that he had been a lieutenant colonel of volunteers. That July he had told Lodge he was not a candidate for the War Department and could not leave Albany. What he wanted next was a second term as governor.

And the letter does not stop there. The second paragraph is the good part:

"The President, when I was at the Dewey dinner at the White House, insisted upon my going to Cincinnati — I mean literally insisted, and would not take no for an answer, so I had to reluctantly accede. He then did his best to get me to go to Nebraska and Iowa, but here I finally refused, for I agree with you that if I went at all I would find it very difficult not to go everywhere."

So: batting away a presidential boom in one sentence, and in the next being hauled around the country by the sitting President.

The friend was Herman Kohlsaat, who owned two Chicago papers, had helped bail McKinley out of a ruinous debt in 1893, and four years before this had sponsored what is usually called America's first automobile race. He was the one telling Roosevelt to stay off the road.

Sixteen days later, to Lodge, from the Union League Club in New York:

"After sending you that Oregon letter yesterday I suddenly thought you might regard it as a sympton of desire on my part to get into the Presidential campaign. Heaven forbid! I wrote the writer at once that of course McKinley was inevitable, and that I was not in the race in any way or shape."

"Sympton" is his spelling.

#OTD in 1905, Theodore Roosevelt set three islands aside for birds in a single day, in orders that begin with four words and no argument.

"It is hereby ordered that…"

No preamble, no whereas, no statute cited. Each one reserves an island "for the use of the Department of Agriculture as a preserve and breeding ground for native birds," and each is dated "The White House, October 10, 1905," over the signature. The numbers you will see attached to them were assigned by compilers decades afterward; Roosevelt never wrote them.

The three were Passage Key, at the mouth of Tampa Bay, and the Huron and Siskiwit islands — both of which are in Lake Superior. The Huron Islands are eight rocks totalling 147 acres, three miles off the Michigan shore.

What was living there, from William Dutcher's president's report for the Audubon societies that year: on Passage Key, "Royal, Cabot's, Least and Sooty Terns. Thousands of Herons and also several varieties of shore-birds breed there." On the Michigan islands, one flat sentence — "large colonies of Herring Gulls, together with a few Ducks."

The first wardens on the Michigan islands were the lighthouse keepers. Their orders came from Commander Charles E. Fox, inspector of the Eleventh Lighthouse District: "You are instructed to aid in protecting the birds about those islands as far as may be, without interfering with your duties as light-house keeper."

It seems to have worked. Dutcher, on the two Michigan colonies: they "had a quiet season, the wardens preventing molestation."

Pelican Island had been the first, two years and seven months earlier. These three brought the count to six.

Siskiwit was folded into Isle Royale National Park by act of Congress in 1942. The Huron Islands are still a refuge, and the whole of it is designated wilderness.

Passage Key is the one to sit with. In 1905 it was a mangrove island with a freshwater lake. A hurricane took the lake in 1921. The island came back, was made a wilderness in 1970, and has washed away again since. It is now a sandbar that is often completely under water at high tide.

It is still a national wildlife refuge. It is still closed to the public.

#OTD in 1910, a former president climbed into an open biplane at a field outside St. Louis, sat down on the wing beside the pilot, and went up. No cockpit. No belt.

He had not planned it. He was on a campaign swing for the Missouri Republicans, and the aviator — Arch Hoxsey of the Wright exhibition team — had set an American distance record three days earlier, flying 104 miles from Springfield, Illinois. By Hoxsey's own account in the New-York Tribune the next morning, he made the offer and Roosevelt took about a second over it.

"Here's your chance."

"All right; let's not make too much fuss about it while I am getting into the machine."

Then two laps of Kinloch Field — about three miles, at something like a hundred feet, in three minutes and twenty seconds. Partway round he caught sight of the grandstand and waved at it, which made the machine wobble.

On the ground he turned to the pilot: "Hoxsey, you're all right!"

To the reporters: "It was great! First class!… I wish I could stay up for an hour, but I haven't the time this afternoon."

And that evening, at the governor's dinner: "That was the bulliest experience I ever had. I envy you, your professional conquest of space."

He was the first American president ever to leave the ground — but the word order matters. He was a *former* president, nineteen months out of office. No sitting president would fly for another thirty-two years, when Franklin Roosevelt crossed the Atlantic to Casablanca in January 1943.

Not quite seven years had passed since Kitty Hawk.

Someone was filming, and the reel survives at the Library of Congress: a fifty-one-year-old ex-president in a cloth cap, being handed up into a machine made of spruce, wire and muslin.

Arch Hoxsey was in his twenties. Eighty-one days later, on the last day of that year, he took a Wright biplane up over Dominguez Field in Los Angeles to beat his own altitude record of 11,474 feet. He was killed in the fall.

#OTD in 1912, a weekly newspaper in Ishpeming, Michigan, printed one sentence about Theodore Roosevelt. Seven months later it cost its publisher six cents and the central charge he had made.

Iron Ore, Saturday, October 12, 1912, under the heading "The Roosevelt Way":

"Roosevelt lies and curses in a most disgusting way; he gets drunk, too, and that not infrequently, and all his intimates know about it."

Most of the editorial is about the other charge — that he called everyone else a liar and could not take it back. It ends: "For so great a fighter, self-styled, he is the poorest loser we ever knew."

Roosevelt sued. He was in Mercy Hospital in Chicago when the papers were filed, with a bullet in his chest from Milwaukee two days after the editorial ran.

The trial opened at Marquette in May 1913. He brought his witnesses north on a train — Jacob Riis, his physicians, three men who had sat in his cabinet — and read in the depositions of a dozen more.

"I have never been drunk or in the slightest degree under the influence of liquor."

"I have never drunk a high-ball or cocktail in my life. I have sometimes drunk mint juleps in the White House. There was a bed of mint there, and I may have drunk half a dozen mint juleps a year, and certainly no more."

On May 31 the publisher, George A. Newett, read a statement. He had taken more than forty depositions. He had found people who would swear they had watched Roosevelt speak and believed he was drunk. He had found no one who had seen it.

"It is fair to the plaintiff to state that I have been unable to find in any section of the country any individual witness who is willing to state that he has personally seen Mr. Roosevelt drink to excess… I am forced to the conclusion that I was mistaken."

The suit had asked $10,000. Roosevelt stood and gave it up on the spot.

"Your Honor, in view of the statement of the defendant, I ask the Court to instruct the jury that I desire only nominal damages.

I did not go into this suit for money. I did not go into it for any vindictive purpose. I went into it, and, as the Court has said, I made my reputation an issue, because I wished, once for all during my lifetime, thoroughly and comprehensively to deal with these slanders, so that never again will it be possible for any man, in good faith, to repeat them.

I have achieved my purpose, and I am content."

Nominal damages under Michigan law were six cents. The court found Newett had published in good faith and without malice.

Two things the record is careful about. Newett was a teetotaler, and he had been postmaster of Ishpeming — an appointment, as he said on the stand, "from the plaintiff in this case."

And he took back only the drinking charge. On the other, Riis testified that he had never heard Roosevelt "use any unclean or profane language," only "the expression 'Godfrey' when he gets very much excited."

#OTD in 1912, at ten past eight at night, Theodore Roosevelt left a Milwaukee hotel, stepped into a waiting car and stood up to raise his hat. A man six feet away shot him in the chest.

His first concern was the man who shot him.

Over a crowd shouting "kill him": "Don't hurt him; bring him to me here!" They dragged the man to the car, and Roosevelt looked at him: "Officers, take charge of him, and see that there is no violence done to him."

He refused the hospital and went to the hall. A stenographer took down what he said to nine thousand people.

"Friends, I shall ask you to be as quiet as possible," he said. "I don't know whether you fully understand that I have just been shot, but it takes more than that to kill a bull moose. (Cheers.) But fortunately I had my manuscript, so you see I was going to make a long speech (holds up manuscript with bullet hole) and there is a bullet — there is where the bullet went through and it probably saved me from it going into my heart."

He was right that it helped, and generous about how much. It had gone through an overcoat, fifty pages of typescript folded double — a hundred thicknesses of paper — a metal spectacle case and a double fold of heavy suspenders. The surgeons put it carefully: its force "was much diminished," and the wound showed "evidence of a much bent bullet."

He spoke for about eighty minutes. Partway through he turned to the stage: "How long have I talked?" Told three-quarters of an hour, he said, "Well, I will take a quarter of an hour more."

Then he said this about the man who shot him:

"Now friends, of course, I do not know, as I say, anything about him, but it is a very natural thing that weak and vicious minds should be inflamed to acts of violence by the kind of awful mendacity and abuse that have been heaped upon me for the last three months by the papers in the interest of not only Mr. Debs but of Mr. Wilson and Mr. Taft."

And then, immediately:

"Friends, I will disown and repudiate any man of my party who attacks with such foul slander and abuse any opponent of any other party."

The bullet lodged between the fourth and fifth ribs, three and a half inches in, just short of the lining of the lung. It was never taken out; it was still there when he died in 1919.

The man was John Flammang Schrank, a former New York saloonkeeper born in Bavaria. Five doctors found him insane. He was never tried, and died in a Wisconsin hospital in 1943.

Taft wired him that he was "greatly shocked to hear of the outrageous and deplorable assault." Wilson kept the engagements already booked, then stopped until Roosevelt could return, having "no desire to be the single candidate on the stump engaged against no active antagonist." Roosevelt, from his hospital bed: "I shall be sorry if Mr. Wilson does not keep on the stump."

He lost the election.

#OTD in 1886, a twenty-seven-year-old was nominated for mayor of New York without being in the room. He found out from a reporter.

The Republican county convention met at the Grand Opera House and named him by acclamation. Theodore Roosevelt was across town at the Union League Club when a man from the Tribune brought him the news.

"It comes to me somewhat in the nature of a surprise, for, until eight o'clock last evening, I had not been spoken to formally on the subject of the nomination for the Mayoralty. While very reluctant to accept it, the matter has been presented to me in such a light as to make me feel it impossible to refuse."

On what the job would take, he was less careful: the man who held it "must be willing and able to use the knife with merciless thoroughness in cutting out the countless already long-existing abuses."

Consider where he was standing. Two years and eight months earlier, his wife and his mother had died in the same house on the same day. He had gone to the Dakota Badlands. He came back east that autumn with a book written and a ranch behind him, and the party handed him a race it did not expect him to win.

It did not. On 2 November the count was Abram Hewitt 90,552, Henry George 68,110, Theodore Roosevelt 60,435. Third, in his own city — and by then he was twenty-eight, the formal ratification having been at Cooper Union on the 27th, his birthday.

And then he did something nobody in that convention hall knew about.

For eleven months he had been secretly engaged to Edith Kermit Carow, a childhood friend, a fact he had kept from almost everyone because a widower remarrying so soon was a thing people talked about. Four days after losing the election he sailed for England on the Cunard liner Etruria. He had booked passage for himself and his sister Bamie as "Mr. and Miss Merrifield" — the name of his Dakota ranch partner.

On 2 December they were married at St George's, Hanover Square, in a London fog so thick that link-bearers had to guide his carriage to the door and the fog hung inside the nave. He wore orange gloves.

One hundred and twenty-five years ago today, Booker T. Washington became the first African American to dine as a guest of the President and his family at the White House.

Every word of that sentence is doing work. Black Americans had been to the White House before — Sojourner Truth met Lincoln in his office in 1864, Frederick Douglass came to the second inaugural reception in 1865, the soprano Marie Selika Williams sang there in 1878. What had not happened was this: a seat at the family table.

Washington had come into Washington by train from a lecture tour in Mississippi and was staying at the house of Whitefield McKinlay on Eleventh Street. The invitation was waiting when he got there. He wrote about it ten years later:

"When I reached Mr. McKinlay's house I found an invitation from President Roosevelt asking me to dine with him at the White House that evening at eight o'clock."

The note Roosevelt actually sent said half past seven. Eight o'clock is Washington's memory, a decade on.

Roosevelt had been President for a month. At the table were Edith, four of the children — Kermit, Ethel, Archie and Quentin — and one other guest, Philip Stewart of Colorado. Washington and Stewart sat on either side of the President.

It was a working dinner. The two men had been corresponding since Roosevelt's first week in office about federal appointments in the South, and that is what they discussed. Washington's own account of the evening is four sentences long:

"At the hour appointed I went to the White House and dined with the President and members of his family and a gentleman from Colorado. After dinner we talked at considerable length concerning plans about the South which the President had in mind. I left the White House almost immediately and took a train the same night for New York."

No photograph of the dinner exists. Two years later a Chicago company printed the last picture in this post — an invented scene, the two men alone at a small round table, Lincoln's portrait on the wall, the word Equality across the cloth. Its own caption dates the dinner to October 17th, which is the day the story broke, not the day it happened. It is not a record of the evening. It is a record of what some Americans wanted the evening to mean.

What happened next was not planned by anyone. The White House gave reporters its routine list of the day's callers, as it did every day. One line went out on the wires overnight.

Booker T. Washington, of Tuskegee, Ala., dined with the President last evening.

Tomorrow: the country reads it.

#OTD in 1901, the country found out that Booker T. Washington had eaten dinner at the White House, and a great many white Americans lost their minds.

It got out because of paperwork. A reporter working the White House late that night found the name on the day's list of callers. One line moved on the wires and ran in the morning papers.

Booker T. Washington, of Tuskegee, Ala., dined with the President last evening.

The Memphis Scimitar called it "the most damnable outrage which has ever been perpetrated by any citizen of the United States." The Richmond Times said it meant Roosevelt saw no reason "why whites and blacks may not marry and intermarry." The Memphis Commercial Appeal: "this is a white man's country. President Roosevelt has committed a blunder that is worse than a crime."

And a sitting United States senator, Benjamin Tillman of South Carolina, said this out loud:

"The action of President Roosevelt in entertaining that nigger will necessitate our killing a thousand niggers in the South before they will learn their place again."

The scale is measurable. In the fifteen days after the dinner, Washington's name appears on 435 pages of the newspapers digitized in the Library of Congress's Chronicling America — 69 of them in the first four days.

That is the half of this story everybody knows. Here is the half that got buried.

The Washington Bee, a Black paper in the capital, put Washington's portrait on its front page that Saturday under the line "No color line in the White House — An Object Lesson for the South." A week later it asked the obvious question: "Hasn't a man the right to invite whom he pleases to his house?"

The Colored American: "President Roosevelt is the Chief Magistrate of the whole people. As such, it was perfectly natural for him to recognize the most conspicious representative of a race constituting one eighth of the population of the United States." (The spelling is theirs.)

The Cleveland Gazette called the dinner "perfectly right and proper," then printed a warning that reads now like prophecy: it "will eventually prove the latter's undoing, as far as his great educational work is concerned."

And on 22 October, at its annual meeting in Oak Park, Illinois, the American Missionary Association adopted — without a dissenting voice — a resolution of approval for a President "thus ignoring race prejudice."

Washington himself said nothing. He never gave an interview about that evening, and when a paper printed one anyway he answered flatly: "I want to state as emphatically as I can that I have given no interview…" He did not write about it until his 1911 memoir.

Roosevelt, privately, at the end of that month: "I shall have him to dine just as often as I please."

He never did.

#OTD in 1905, four years after the dinner, Theodore Roosevelt boarded a train for the South.

It left Washington at half past eight in the morning. Fredericksburg just after ten. Ashland for three minutes, long enough for the Randolph-Macon College students. Richmond by noon. He spoke in Capitol Square that afternoon, and at the luncheon that followed he said this:

"Next only to a man's having worn the blue comes the fact of the man's having worn the gray, as entitling him to honor in my sight."

Two days later he was at Roswell, Georgia. He walked through the house where his mother grew up, then spoke in the town park.

"It has been my very great good fortune to have the right to claim that my blood is half Southern and half Northern."

He meant it literally. Martha Bulloch was a Georgia girl; her brothers served the Confederacy, and one of them, Irvine, was — Roosevelt told the crowd — the man who fired the last two shots from the raider Alabama before she went down off Cherbourg. He told that story to a Georgia crowd, about his own uncle, as President of the United States.

The tour ran nine days through seven states and ended at New Orleans. The press called it a triumph.

Here is what he did not say, in nine days, in a run of speeches that fills a volume.

He did not mention disfranchisement. Between 1889 and 1908 every state of the former Confederacy rewrote its constitution or its statutes to strip Black men of the vote they had been guaranteed in 1870. It was happening while he spoke. He said nothing about it on that trip.

And ten months later, after a night shooting in Brownsville, Texas that no one was ever tried for, he discharged 167 Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry without honor and without a hearing. The Army reversed it in 1972. One of the men, Dorsie Willis of Minneapolis, was still alive to receive his discharge — on his eighty-seventh birthday.

The man who set a place at his table in 1901 is the same man. Both things are the record.

By evening the same four signatures were back, and the tone had changed:

"To-night the patient is fatigued from having undertaken to respond to some of the importunities of his friends. While he has to-day probably passed the crisis he is not at all beyond the range of danger... On this day in 1903, Theodore Roosevelt sat down in the White House to answer a letter from his sixteen-year-old son.

Ted had written from Groton about winning his place on the football field among the older boys — and about how, having won it, he had gone and lost his perspective.

His father told him he had done the same thing, and worse.

"I never did well enough in athletics while a boy to get such a position, either at school or college; but immediately after leaving college I went to the legislature. I was the youngest man there, and I rose like a rocket. I was re-elected next year by an enormous majority in a time when the republican party as a whole met with great disaster; and the republican minority in the house, although I was the youngest member, nominated me for speaker, that is, made me the leader of the minority. I immediately proceeded to lose my perspective, also. Unfortunately, I did not recover it as early as you have done in this case, and the result was that I came an awful cropper and had to pick myself up after learning by bitter experience the lesson that I was not all-important and that I had to take account of many different elements in life."

And then: "It took me fully a year before I got back the position I had lost, but I hung steadily at it and achieved my purpose."

The line is worth getting right, because it travels attached to the wrong story. "I rose like a rocket" is not about a treaty or an election or the presidency. It is about Albany, twenty years earlier, and a young man who got above himself. It is also, as he tells it, a little compressed — Columbia Law School and a marriage came between Harvard and the Assembly seat.

The same letter runs on to the Alaska boundary award, handed down in London that day, which settled the central question in America's favor: a continuous coastal strip, cutting Canada off from tidewater. There he takes credit, and does not whisper it. "I declined absolutely to allow any arbitration of the matter... a straight-out declaration to certain high British officials that I meant business."

One letter, one afternoon at one desk. A father telling his son he once came an awful cropper, and in the next breath telling him how he had just won.

On this day in 1903, Theodore Roosevelt wrote a journalist a letter he later refused to let him print in full.

Ray Stannard Baker had a piece in the November McClure's — "The Trust's New Tool — The Labor Boss" — arguing that trusts and employers had bought the labor bosses of the New York building trades. Roosevelt read it and replied that week, marking his letter "Private and personal."

"I am immensely impressed by your article. While I had known in rather a vague way that there was such a condition as you describe, I had not known its extent, and as far as I am aware the facts have never before been brought before the public in such striking fashion."

Then he set out how the whole thing looked to him:

"The organs of the Wall Street men of a certain type are bitter in their denunciations of the labor unions, and have not a word to say against the iniquity of the corporations. The labor leaders of a certain type howl against the corporations, but do not admit that there is any wrong ever perpetrated by labor men."

He named a Democrat, Richard Olney, and a Republican official he was preparing to indict. And then this:

"And I regret to say that high Republican politicians come to me and beg me not to expose Republican rascality, lest it may hurt the party; while men standing high in the business circles of New York, — men whom I know socially, — follow a course of conduct which, in its essence, is as immoral as that of any boodle alderman."

A boodle alderman was period slang for a city councilman on the take. The New York businessmen he leaves unnamed.

Five weeks later Baker asked whether he could publish it. Roosevelt said no to the letter — "I do not think my entire letter to you could be used with advantage" — and then made one exception: "but I see no objection to your using this paragraph of it":

"I believe in corporations; I believe in trade unions. Both have come to stay, and are necessities in our present industrial system. But where, in either the one or the other, there develops corruption or mere brutal indifference to the rights of others, and shortsighted refusal to look beyond the moment's gain, then the offender, whether union or corporation, must be fought, and if the public sentiment is calloused to the iniquity of either, by just so much the whole public is damaged."

That is the paragraph a President cleared for print. The rest of it stayed in the file.

On this day in 1903, the President of the United States spent the afternoon lying on a sofa.

He described it the next afternoon in a letter to Kermit, away at Groton:

"Yesterday I felt rather seedy, having a touch of Cuban fever, my only unpleasant reminiscence of the Santiago campaign. Accordingly I spent the afternoon in the house lying on the sofa, with a bright fire burning and Mother in the rocking chair, with her knitting, beside me. I felt so glad that I was not out somewhere in the wilderness, campaigning or hunting, where I would have to walk or ride all day in the rain and then lie out under a bush at night!"

Every detail there is his own — the sofa, the bright fire, the rocking chair, the knitting. Nothing has been added by a biographer. A man with a lifelong reputation for never sitting still, glad of a fire and his wife's company, and saying so plainly to his fourteen-year-old son.

He had worked that Friday morning. The cabinet met, thinly — four of nine members turned up. Senator Shelby Cullom came in on Cuban reciprocity. John Landis, Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint, was called in over civil service violations at the Mint. And Charles Walcott, Director of the Geological Survey, just back from three months in the West, talked irrigation and forestry, and was told the President would take up both in his annual message.

No contemporaneous newspaper account reports him unwell. Outside the family, nobody knew.

"Cuban fever" is his phrase and his own attribution — period language, not a diagnosis. Our archives partner files the letter under "Malaria"; the letter itself never uses the word. He said it came back from time to time, and he blamed Santiago.

The rest of it is a dog named Ronald who has won golden opinions, Quentin learning to ride the pony and taking a tumble he judged no worse than a pillow fight, and the message to Congress: "All of this work is terribly puzzling at times, but I peg away at it, and every now and then, when the dust clears away and I look around, I feel that I really have accomplished a little at any rate."

On this day in 1894, Theodore Roosevelt wrote Henry Cabot Lodge a letter that Lodge, thirty-one years later, chose not to print.

Roosevelt was thirty-five, three days short of his birthday, a Civil Service Commissioner in Washington. New York Republicans had wanted him for Mayor. He had said no — and then watched the campaign happen without him.

"The last four weeks, ever since I decided not to run, have been pretty bitter ones for me; I would literally have given my right arm to have made the race, win or lose. It was the one golden chance, which never returns; and I had no illusions about ever having another opportunity. I knew it meant the definite abandonment of any hope of going on in the work and life for which I care more than any other; but outside of my immediate family no one but you knows this."

Then he named the reason, and refused to hide behind it:

"At the time, with Edith feeling as intensely as she did, I did not see how I could well go in; though I have grown to feel more and more that in this instance I should have gone counter to her wishes and made the race anyhow. It is not necessary to say to you that the fault was mine, not Edith's; I should have realized that she could not see the matter as it really was, or realize my feelings. But it is one of the matters just as well dropped..."

Edith's objection was not the cost. She did not want to leave Washington, and she would not stake the family's security on an office he could be voted out of. Four weeks on, he is still writing that he feels it "more and more" — and two days before this letter he had told his sister Bamie: "No outsider should know that I think my decision was a mistake."

He never wrote about it for the public. In 1897 he published a long Atlantic essay on the very election that swept Tammany out of City Hall, and never mentioned that he had been asked to lead the ticket. The Autobiography skips it too.

It survives in the letters, and barely. In 1925 Lodge published two volumes of their correspondence. From 1894 he printed 2 September, 30 September, 2 October, 8 October, 11 October, 16 October, 27 October and 1 December. He printed the tidy explanation from the 8th — "I simply had not the funds to run" — and the stoic silver lining from the 27th. He left out the 24th. Bamie had published her own volume of his letters the year before, and left the episode out as well.

Both of the people he trusted with it edited it away.

The following spring a reform mayor named him one of four police commissioners. On his first day, 6 May 1895, the board elected him its president.

The friend was Philip B. Stewart, one of his companions on a five-week cougar hunt out of Meeker, in the White River country of northwestern Colorado, that January — and the man who took the photographs.

What makes the letter worth reading is everything around that paragraph. The dinner is the first of four topics. Next comes a cheque: "I enclose you my check for $150 as your share of the Scribner's articles... I am inclined to think I am doing you an injustice; but it is perfectly useless to ask you to tell me if I am, so I have just got to take the chances!" Then: "John Greenway is staying with me, and I am thoroughly enjoying him." Then: "I was received at Yale in a way that really did me good."

And then, in his own hand across the second page, Colorado patronage. Would Stewart go and see Edward Kent, the assistant U.S. district attorney in Denver, and go over some of the appointments — "or rather the character of the appointees. He is a gentleman." On Senator Henry Teller, a Silver Republican by then fighting his own former party: "I fear I cannot take his statements save with careful discount for his bitter party prejudices."

That is what the storm looked like from the inside. Nine days in, with the papers still at it — that week the Raleigh News & Observer ran a fresh editorial headed "Booker Washington Again" — and the President is amused, unrepentant, settling up with a friend over photographs, and getting on with the appointments.

On this day in 1904, thirteen days before the election, Theodore Roosevelt wrote his campaign chairman a letter marked Confidential.

"I have just been informed that the Standard Oil people have contributed one hundred thousand dollars to our campaign fund. This may be entirely untrue. But if true I must ask you to direct that the money be returned to them forthwith."

He demanded it three more times over the next three days, ending: "Has my request been complied with? I desire that there be no delay."

Eight years later, John D. Archbold of Standard Oil testified under oath that he had handed the money to the party treasurer in currency, in thousand-dollar bills — and that it had never come back.

Roosevelt appeared in person on 3 October 1912, eleven days before he was shot in Milwaukee, and read his own letters into the record. He still would not concede that the money had ever been taken. "I have never said either that I did or did not believe that it was made."

The order is a matter of record, in his own letterpress book, signed in his own hand. What became of the money is not. Archbold swore it was never returned and that no one ever asked him to take it back. Bliss and Cortelyou told Roosevelt it had never been received at all. On the afternoon of 28 October 1886, in the rain, New York unveiled the Bartholdi Statue in its harbor. There were parades on land and water, and the French delegation reached Bedloe's Island at a quarter to three. The illumination and the fireworks planned for that night were postponed on account of the weather.

Theodore Roosevelt spent the evening speaking in halls on the West Side.

He had turned 28 the day before. He was the Republican candidate for Mayor, and he would finish third. The Times and the Tribune both filed on the night, which leaves a record of what the day the statue went up looked like from inside a political meeting.

He took a hansom from the Fifth Avenue Hotel to the Grand Opera House Hall at Eighth Avenue and Twenty-third Street. Partway through, the music started. The Times man wrote it down:

"The sound of fife and drum floated up stairs, and the next few sentences of Mr. Roosevelt were unintelligible. Two hundred Germans, with the fifer and drummer at their head, each working away for dear life, marched into the room, down one aisle, along in front of the platform, and back the other aisle to seats on the side of the hall."

The Tribune's reporter supplies what Roosevelt said once the music stopped: "When I first heard that music I thought it was a belated remnant of the Bartholdi Statue celebration, but I find it leads a procession of new supporters."

Of the two papers that covered the meeting, only the Tribune prints that line. The Times does not quote him here at all — it notes only that he returned to his subject "after acknowledging their complimentary attention." The two accounts fit together.

The colored voters of the Eleventh Assembly District had organized a parade of their own — a brass band and a truck, as the Times put it, "just blazing with Chinese lanterns" — and the line of march "had been extended beyond all bounds." So he left, spoke uptown at the Boulevard and Sixty-seventh Street, and came back to try again. By then they had come in off the streets.

Three speeches, four stops.

From June 1902 the Roosevelts did not live in the White House. Charles McKim had gutted it.

On 5 November they came back. The President stopped in Philadelphia to speak on the way; he and Edith and the two youngest boys, Archie and Quentin, reached Washington at twenty past seven that evening and slept in the house for the first time since the summer. He was at his desk in the new offices west of the house by half past nine the next morning.

The Evening Star, reporting it, put the state of the place carefully: "The improvements throughout the building are still incomplete, but there is sufficient completed space for the accommodation of the household for the present."

Which is a generous way of saying the lower floor was still a building site. He left again for New York the following Monday.

The room that had changed most was the State Dining Room. McKim had pulled out the grand staircase and pushed the room into its footprint, making a room that could seat more than a hundred.

That sharpened a problem the house had been quietly carrying for a century. An inventory made the year before, under McKinley, had found very little china left from previous administrations — certainly nothing that would set a table for a hundred.

What Edith Roosevelt did about that is why there is a White House china collection. She ordered a Wedgwood service of 1,344 pieces. She had cabinets built in the ground-floor corridor where visitors could see the older china. She ruled that nothing be bought — only given or lent. She had the collection made official government property so that it could never be dispersed. And she directed that broken pieces be destroyed rather than sold at auction — TR's military aide Archie Butt wrote that she thought that method "cheapens the White House."

The idea was not originally hers. Caroline Harrison had wanted a cabinet built for the china a decade earlier and died before it happened. But the collection is Edith's doing, and it begins in a house still too full of builders' dust to lay a table properly.

The Cunard liner Etruria was advertised to leave Pier 40, North River, at one o'clock on Saturday 6 November 1886. Mails closed at ten. Cabin passage was $60, $80 and $100.

Four days after losing the New York mayoral election, Theodore Roosevelt went aboard her. The Times listed the party the next morning — "Mr. and Mrs. Douglas Robinson, Miss Roosevelt, and Mr. Theodore Roosevelt" — his sister Corinne and her husband, his sister Bamie, and him. They were going over for his wedding.

Somewhere on the same ship was a young British diplomat named Cecil Spring Rice. He had been told in advance that the Roosevelts would be aboard and that he should go and introduce himself. He did.

Writing home about the crossing, Spring Rice described his new acquaintance:

"I came over with Roosevelt, who has been standing for the mayoralty of New York against H. George and who is supposed to be the boss Republican young man. He is going to be married and then to be in England in February so that you will see him, I hope."

Twenty-six days later, Spring Rice was best man at the wedding.

The Etruria was not the only ship due out of the North River at one o'clock that afternoon. The French liner La Gascogne was leaving at the same hour, carrying Ferdinand de Lesseps and part of the French delegation home from the unveiling of the Statue of Liberty nine days earlier. The Etruria took the lead, and La Gascogne, in the Times' phrase, "quietly waited until she was well under way before she followed her."

The Sun put the sailing on its front page the next morning. He was, it said, "accompanied to the steamer by many of his family and friends and sent off with warm wishes and congratulations."

A week later, at twenty to twelve on the morning of Saturday 13 November, the Etruria reached Queenstown.

Eleven days married. Theodore Roosevelt's diary for Sunday 7 November 1880, in his own hand — this is the whole entry:

"In the morning I read aloud from the bible; in the afternoon we took a long walk through woods and fields, in the beautiful, clear, cool Autumn weather. Alice is a beautiful walker, with her long, firm step, and clambers over fences about as easily as I do.

My old hunter keeps us pretty well supplied with woodcock & partridge."

It is the second sentence that does the work. A twenty-two-year-old noting, apparently with pleasure, that his wife can keep up with him and get over a fence as easily as he can.

The day before, rain had kept them indoors: "I love to talk over everything with Baby, from Politics to Poetry, and to read aloud to her, either from a History or standard novel or from the daily newspaper that forms our only intercourse with the outside world."

That same Sunday morning the White Star liner Germanic was finally getting to sea. She had been advertised out on the Saturday, but a storm and then dense fog held the whole European fleet at their piers — her captain would not take her through it. She left on the Sunday, and as she passed the light-ship she struck a Dutch ship, the Samarang, which had hove to there to drop her pilot.

Aboard the Germanic, according to Geoffrey Ward's life of the young Franklin Roosevelt, were James Roosevelt and Sara Delano, a month into their own honeymoon — they had married on 7 October. James was Theodore's fourth cousin once removed. Their son Franklin, born in January 1882, would be Theodore's fifth cousin.
